restatements.text: States the measure's purpose is to require audits of programs receiving new or higher special taxes and to prohibit exemptions from the state spending limit.

Requires the California State Auditor to prepare a pre-election financial and performance audit for any proposed special tax initiative, detailing potential savings, waste, and goal achievement, with an executive summary printed in the voter guide. The Auditor is reimbursed from the tax revenue if the measure passes.
Requires the State Auditor to conduct ongoing financial and performance audits every four years for programs receiving money from new or higher special taxes enacted after January 1, 2026.

Prohibits any state tax enacted or taking effect after January 1, 2026, from being exempted or excluded from the constitutional Government Spending Limitation, and forbids the state from collecting any tax that attempts such an exemption.
Declares that if this measure receives more votes than a conflicting measure on the same ballot, the conflicting measure is entirely null and void.

Requires the Attorney General to appoint independent counsel to defend the measure if the Governor and Attorney General refuse to do so, and creates a continuous General Fund appropriation to cover the counsel's costs.

analysis.answer: Current law is not provided. The measure requires the California State Auditor to perform deep-dive financial and performance audits (including recommending 10% savings) before any special tax initiative goes to voters, and requires the executive summary of this audit to be printed in the state voter guide.

Current law is not provided. The measure categorically prohibits any state tax enacted after January 1, 2026 from being exempted from the state's constitutional Government Spending Limitation (often known as the Gann Limit), preventing a mechanism previously used to bypass state revenue caps.

There will be direct administrative and opportunity costs for the State Auditor to conduct extensive pre-election audits on short timelines. The text states costs will be reimbursed from the special tax revenue if approved by voters, implying that if the initiative fails, the audit cost is absorbed by the state.

There is a massive opportunity cost in state revenues: by forcing all new taxes under the spending limit, it caps the state's capacity to collect and spend funds once the overall limit is hit, meaning public services forgo funding that might otherwise have been raised through exempted taxes.

Taxpayers broadly benefit from reduced exposure to new taxes, as total state revenue growth will be strictly capped. Programs and populations reliant on state-funded public services bear the cost, as the state loses flexibility to raise dedicated funds when hitting the spending limit.

Initiative proponents may try to structure proposals as 'general taxes' rather than 'special taxes' to bypass the new pre-election audit and voter guide summary requirements. The State Auditor may experience severe workload crunches right before ballot qualification deadlines.

The text asserts that taxpayers fund ineffective and wasteful programs and that special interests repeatedly bypass spending limits. The mechanism attempts to fix this by imposing public audits to highlight inefficiencies and by enforcing a strict constitutional ban on spending-limit exemptions.

The California State Auditor gains significant influence, as their executive summaries—including assessments of waste, fraud, and recommendations for 10% cuts—will be printed directly in the official voter guide for every proposed special tax, strongly shaping voter perception.

The long-term effects of strict constitutional spending limits are disputed. Some researchers find they effectively constrain government growth and force prioritization of essential services; others find they degrade public infrastructure and services by structurally preventing revenues from keeping pace with economic growth or population needs.
The direct cost of the audits themselves represents administrative overhead that will be deducted from the special tax revenues if the measure passes.
This adds Article XXIV to the California Constitution, meaning it can only be undone or modified by another constitutional amendment approved by voters.

flags.quote: Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in Chapter 6 (commencing with Section 12500) of Part 2 of Division 3 of Title 2 of the Government Code or any other law, the Attorney General shall appoint independent counsel
flags.note: Overrides existing law regarding the Attorney General's standard discretion or duties in legal defense.

flags.quote: if this Act is approved by the voters of the State of California and thereafter subjected to a legal challenge... and both the Governor and Attorney General refuse to defend this Act to the fullest extent possible
flags.note: The mandate to appoint independent counsel and utilize the continuous appropriation is contingent on the Governor and Attorney General refusing to defend the Act.

flags.quote: (t) If the special tax initiative is approved by voters, the California State Auditor shall be reimbursed from the revenue generated by the special tax initiative for reasonable costs incurred in preparing the pre-election financial and performance audit
flags.note: Requires the Auditor to conduct pre-election audits but only authorizes reimbursement from the tax revenue if the initiative passes, effectively creating an unfunded mandate for audits on failed initiatives.

flags.quote: The provisions of this Act are severable.
This Act shall take effect at the earliest possible date in accordance with Section 10 of Article II of the California Constitution.
flags.note: Specifies that the Act takes effect at the earliest possible date allowed by the Constitution.

flags.quote: require the California State Auditor to conduct upfront and ongoing audits... while also prohibiting exemptions from the state spending limit
flags.note: Bundles transparency and auditing requirements for special taxes with a separate, broader constitutional limit on overall state spending capabilities.
